Evaluation scope and ordering: Nine checkpoint evaluations, 27,000 scored episodes: Light-WAM Long (1,500); LoopWAM full 4/4 (6,000); Long 4/4 original, Long 4/4 repeat, KV mix 4/1, aligned 4/1, KV concat 4/1 (1,500 each); original Fast-WAM all suites (6,000); LoopWAM full video1/action4 (6,000). Fast-WAM starts only after concat and the original six-stage campaign complete; video1/action4 starts only after Fast-WAM completes. Diagnostic benchmarks are excluded from scored results.

All branches are inventoried and reviewed. Only the pinned revisions listed as executed are evaluated. A branch review is not an independent evaluation of every branch tip. The trained checkpoint, configuration and compatible model code determine the evaluated variant.
Exact shared rollout protocol: Suites: libero_spatial, libero_object, libero_goal and libero_10 (Long), ten tasks each. Seeds: 42, 43, 44. Each task/seed uses official initial states 0 through 49, exactly once: 500 episodes per suite/seed and 1,500 per suite/model. Seed 45 is confined to the new LoopWAM diagnostic worker benchmark and never enters the scored grid.

Global Python/NumPy/Torch seed is set once for each task/seed group. The environment receives env.seed(base seed) at construction and is reused across 50 episodes. Each episode calls reset then set_init_state. Neither episode seeds nor action-query seeds are incremented; action queries receive the same base seed. This preserves the Light-WAM baseline behavior.

Thirty settling actions [0,0,0,0,0,0,-1] precede policy control. The original loop ignores done during settling and proceeds; this inherited limitation is preserved in all models. Policy caps are 400 steps for Spatial/Object/Goal and 700 for Long. The 32-action prediction horizon executes ten actions before replanning.

Success is the LIBERO environment done flag, which LIBERO step sets from _check_success(). Reaching the external policy-step cap without done is failure. Successes are counted once per episode. Evaluation uses simulator observations only, no ground-truth future video or action ensembling.

Two 256x256 camera renders are rotated 180 degrees, resized to 224x224 and concatenated horizontally to 448x224. Proprioception is eight dimensions: EEF position (3), quaternion converted to axis angle (3), gripper joints (2). Action is seven dimensions: six EEF controls and one gripper control. Each checkpoint uses its released action/state normalization statistics. Gripper conversion is sign(-(2*denormalized_gripper-1)); an exact zero remains zero. No extra action clipping is added.

Videos remain enabled. Persistent workers reuse models and process complete task/seed groups; group scheduling changes throughput without reseeding episodes or shuffling their official initial-state sequence.
Native model inference and fairness: Light-WAM uses its native direct action decoder. LoopWAM uses the native strict constructor and released loop/KV configuration, FP32 policy parameters with BF16 autocast and BF16 Wan2.1 VAE; ten action denoising steps, guidance scale 1 and timestep shift 1. Original Fast-WAM uses native BF16 policy and Wan2.2 VAE; ten denoising steps, guidance scale 1 and timestep shift 5. Native scheduler settings are preserved rather than forcing different trained models into one scheduler.

LoopWAM has 12 physical blocks; four loops give effective depth 30 and one loop gives depth 12. Parameters are shared across repeated depth. Video1/action4 uses one video cache loop with the deeper action cache mapping clamped to the available video cache. KV mix has additional learned mixing parameters; exact counts are read separately from each export.

Light-WAM and LoopWAM use floating-point Torch resizing with antialiasing before BF16 model execution. Fast-WAM retains its native PIL resizing and BF16 pixel normalization. Geometry and camera orientation match, while numerical pixel preprocessing does differ. Therefore the comparison matches simulator protocol and retains native policies; it does not establish identical preprocessing, precision, architecture or training.

Text embeddings are regenerated with the same Wan T5 encoder as the Light-WAM online encoder (SHA256 7cace0da2b446bbbbc57d031ab6cf163a3d59b366da94e5afe36745b746fd81d), batch one, BF16, length 128 and whitespace cleaning. Prompt template: A video recorded from a robot's point of view executing the following instruction: {task}. Forty task-specific caches have integrity hashes and valid token counts. Original LoopWAM training text-cache bytes were not released, so original byte identity cannot be verified. LoopWAM retains its validity mask and zero padded embeddings; Fast-WAM retains zero padded embeddings with its native all-ones attention mask.

Full-suite LoopWAM training manifests contain 1,712 available demonstrations rather than an assumed 2,000. Long-only runs use 344 training and 44 validation demonstrations. Training scope and normalization differ between full-suite and Long-only models. Their SR differences cannot be attributed solely to loop structure. Exact exported epochs, steps, batches, seeds and training times appear in the checkpoint appendix.

Policy parameter counts exclude the VAE and T5 text encoder; total instantiated counts include the VAE but exclude offline T5. Shared modules are deduplicated. Light-WAM policy: 1,859,926,903; VAE: 126,892,531; total: 1,986,819,434. Fast-WAM policy: 6,020,710,599; VAE: 704,688,668; total: 6,725,399,267. Loop counts are taken from each export. The Light-WAM counting log does not establish the actual training freeze schedule; its trainable label is not used as an audited training count.

Original Fast-WAM is explicitly the pinned historical official code snapshot 8afd20f with action shift 5. Current main 7faa711 defaults to shift 1. The source configuration does not prove the released checkpoint historical training shift, and the checkpoint loader does not restore scheduler settings. Its historical training seed and demonstration count are not independently verified.
Timing definitions and speed optimizatio: Production wall time is measured from the model evaluation process, includes worker startup and episode/video work, and excludes predecessor queue waiting. Queue wall times include waiting and must not be interpreted as inference speed. Concurrent worker query durations overlap and cannot be summed to derive wall time.

LoopWAM episode query_seconds starts after observation preprocessing and ends before action denormalization (including synchronized output transfer). Fast-WAM query_seconds wraps the entire native prediction including preprocessing and action conversion. These recorded means have different boundaries and are reported separately. Light-WAM historical outputs lack per-episode steps, query count and query latency; those fields remain unavailable. Baseline task durations and overall wall time are available.

Single-worker eager/graph preflight measurements are provided separately, with warm-up and native model configurations. CUDA graph replay uses the unchanged native video-prefill and action-denoising computations. Every input is copied before replay; static shapes, dtypes, device and constants are checked. Production graph use requires its gate; Fast-WAM and the final Loop variant may fall back to eager when parity fails or graph replay is slower.

Existing six LoopWAM graph gates have zero maximum observed output difference on finite real-observation checks. A separate six-episode eager/graph rollout control matches success, policy steps and query count. This is finite validation rather than proof for all inputs. The final report includes the actual Fast-WAM and video1/action4 gates after they run.

Eight persistent workers and two Torch CPU threads were selected for the existing LoopWAM campaign from tested alternatives. Fast-WAM memory limits cap candidates at four workers; measured diagnostic throughput selects the production count. Video1/action4 benchmarks six versus eight workers. Benchmarks use two representative Long tasks and are a practical speed choice, not proof of globally maximal speed. No reduced denoising, quantization or altered checkpoint tensors is used.
Correctness audit and evidence: Read-only code review found no demonstrated new defect invalidating SR in the reviewed paths. Strict checkpoint loading and SHA validation prevent silent random policy parameters. The matched runners retain the original Light-WAM episode loop; adapters preserve each native policy path. Fast-WAM constructor loading disables unnecessary downloads, then strictly loads original policy and proprioception weights.

Code evidence: Light-WAM experiments/libero/eval_libero_single.py (episode loop); experiments/libero/libero_utils.py (camera rotation/env seed); third_party/LIBERO/libero/libero/envs/bddl_base_domain.py (_check_success and seeding); LoopWAM scripts/evaluate_matched_lightwam.py (group lifecycle, model-only timing); FastWAM scripts/evaluate_matched_lightwam.py (whole prediction timing); scripts/matched_cuda_graph.py (copy/replay); LoopWAM src/fastwam/models/wan22/loop_mot.py (cache mapping); FastWAM scripts/matched_fastwam.py (native text mask and strict policy). Source hashes and branch diffs are archived.

Original matched LoopWAM tests passed (six tests), upstream regression checks passed (86), new variant/queue checks passed (seven), and Fast-WAM CPU checks passed (nine). These are setup-time observations, not a claim of exhaustive model verification. GPU correctness gates for queued models remain required before scoring.

Ordering guards require the original campaign to finish all six stages with 13,500 episodes including concat 1,500, then Fast-WAM all four suites 6,000, before video1/action4. Standalone new-variant commands can bypass the scheduling guard; the running queue enforces it. The report job additionally checks completion statuses and reconstructs every expected scored episode key.

Final report validation rejects missing/duplicate keys, invalid success types, mismatched checkpoint identities, initial-state index mismatches and inconsistent persisted summary totals. Per-suite and per-seed counts are recomputed from raw episode outcomes. Light-WAM binary records are reconstructed from disjoint success/failure index lists and checked against historical summaries.
Interpreting scores and limitations: SR is successes divided by scored episodes, reported as percentages and integer counts. Seed variability is descriptive across three seeds; the same initial-state indices are reused across seeds. Trials and seeds should not be treated as 1,500 independent task samples for strong significance claims. No paper-seed equivalence is assumed. Full-suite macro SR equals episode-weighted SR here because every suite has 1,500 trials.

Long comparisons are paired by suite, task, base seed and official initial-state index. Paired contingency counts describe both succeed, both fail and one-model-only successes; model-dependent trajectories and noise still differ. Light-WAM has no evaluated Spatial/Object/Goal baseline in this campaign, so its all-suite score is unavailable.

Runtime depends on episode lengths and failure caps as well as inference speed. Lower wall time alone is not evidence of a faster model when SR and rollout lengths differ. Production aggregate policy steps/sec and queries/sec are supplied where raw telemetry exists. Query duration percentiles are percentiles of per-episode mean query duration, not individual-query percentiles.

All available branch tips at audit time are documented. Latest Loop KV branch inference source matches the pinned evaluation revision; official latest Fast-WAM has evaluation/manager changes and is not the executed original checkpoint snapshot. This is an audit of available branches, not a claim that every branch was separately run. Remote branches may change after the timestamp recorded in the inventory.
